title: The Cold Hangzhou Flat Where Jack Ma Asked His Friends to Start Again
dek: In February 1999, back from Beijing after two stalled ventures, Jack Ma gathered friends in his flat, filmed the meeting and asked them to begin Alibaba with him.

story.event: The filmed meeting in Ma's Hangzhou flat where the founding team agreed to start Alibaba
story.summary: On 21 February 1999, after his first internet ventures had stalled and a spell in a government-linked job in Beijing, Jack Ma gathered friends and former colleagues in his flat at Lakeside Gardens in Hangzhou and had the meeting filmed. He told them their competitors were in Silicon Valley, warned of painful years ahead and asked them to build a marketplace for small exporters. The team worked from the flat for months; a first fundraising trip to California failed, and in October 1999 a Goldman Sachs-led group invested $5 million.
paragraphs: On 21 February 1999, in a flat at Lakeside Gardens in Hangzhou, Jack Ma seated a group of friends and former colleagues in a semicircle and arranged for the meeting to be filmed. The flat was damp and cold, and some kept their coats on, according to Duncan Clark, who advised the young company and later wrote its history. Ma, a former English teacher, had already tried the internet twice. His first company, China Pages, had been pushed into a joint venture with China Telecom and slipped from his control; a second, Infoshare, had also failed to keep up with bigger rivals. He had then taken a government-linked internet job in Beijing, and several of the people in the room had followed him there.

Coming home meant starting again with very little. Ma later recalled the day they carried their luggage in: they would eat, sleep and work there, probably for a year, and either achieve something or "go out looking for jobs together." China had about two million internet users, and the big portals were already well ahead. Ma chose not to chase them. He would serve small businesses, which he called shrimp, rather than the large companies American trading sites courted.

On the tape he told the group their competitors were "not in China, but in Silicon Valley", and that a company keeping office hours would never succeed. He did not promise ease. He expected "a very painful price in the next three to five years," while aiming for a stock-market listing within three. Then he offered a second reason to stay: "When we charge forward, even if we lose, we still have the team." Eighteen people, six of them women, are counted as Alibaba's founders.

The first test went badly. Ma and Joe Tsai, who had left a finance job to join, flew to California to meet venture capitalists without a pitch book; Clark records the trip as a failure. The team worked from the flat for about seven months, by the account of Porter Erisman, an early employee who later made a documentary about the company. In October 1999 a Goldman Sachs-led group invested $5 million. In 2014 Alibaba was still sending teams of staff to work in the flat.

quote.text: we ought to summon our friends readily to share our good fortunes (for the beneficent character is a noble one), but summon them to our bad fortunes with hesitation; for we ought to give them as little a share as possible in our evils
quote.source_title: Nicomachean Ethics, tr. W. D. Ross, The Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
quote.connection: Ma asked his friends into a venture whose outcome nobody could see, and offered the team itself as the consolation if they lost. Aristotle would call friends into hard times only with hesitation. The story cannot tell us whether that winter evening was an invitation to good fortune or to bad.

reflection: Ma did not hide the cost from the people in his flat. He told them, on camera, to expect painful years. What he could not do was make the risk smaller for them by wanting the company more.

You may be asking people to carry some of what you are building: a colleague giving evenings, a family absorbing your tiredness, a first customer trusting something unfinished. Aristotle's caution is not a reason to stop asking. It is a reason to ask plainly, to say what it may cost them, and to notice when what you are asking has quietly grown.
invitation: Think of one person who is sharing the cost of your work without having had much say in it. Today, tell them plainly what the next few months may ask of them, and ask what they need.

cross_checks.claim: In early 1999 Ma gathered his co-founders in his Hangzhou flat and the meeting was filmed (the footage later appeared in Crocodile in the Yangtze).
Ma told the team their competitors were not in China but in Silicon Valley.
Alibaba had 18 founders: Ma and 17 others.
Before Alibaba, China Pages had failed, and Ma had worked in a government-linked internet job in Beijing that some of the team followed him to.
In October 1999 a Goldman Sachs-led group invested $5 million.
Six of the 18 founders were women.

research_notes: The exact date (21 February 1999), the cold, the coats and the semicircle come only from Duncan Clark's book (excerpted in The National) and are attributed to him; other sources say only '1999'. The 1999 speech survives in two English renderings: Clark's translation and the subtitles of Porter Erisman's film Crocodile in the Yangtze (quoted by Fortune and Mothership). They differ in wording ('not in China, but in Silicon Valley' versus 'not in China but in America's Silicon Valley'; the 8am-5pm line), so every quotation from the speech is taken from Clark's text, and the 8am-5pm remark is paraphrased. Ma's 'go out looking for jobs together' is from his own 2019 recollection in Alibaba's video, quoted by CNBC. Headcount: Alibaba Group and CNBC say 18 founders (Ma plus 17); CNN's timeline says Ma co-founded it 'with 18 others' and Market Realist says his wife plus 16 friends; the story uses 18 including Ma. Funding: Clark says a Goldman Sachs-led group took 50 per cent for $5 million by October 1999; Business Insider (2014) says $5 million from Goldman and $20 million from SoftBank 'by October 1999', whereas Wikipedia dates the SoftBank money to January 2000; the story gives only the October 1999 Goldman-led $5 million. A widely repeated figure of 500,000 yuan pooled by the founders is unsourced on Wikipedia and could not be found in a loading source, so it is not used; 'bootstrapped' describes the episode itself (no outside investors until October 1999). Time in the flat: Fortune reports Erisman's film as saying seven months; Ma in 2019 said they planned for 'probably' a year; the story gives Erisman's figure as his. The Beijing post: Wikipedia and NST describe it as running an IT company for the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation; NST dates Eddie Wu's move to Beijing to 1997 and Wikipedia dates Ma's post to 1998-99, so the story gives no year. The Business Insider (businessinsider.in) pages about the 1999 speech do not load and alizila.com returns 403, so neither is cited. The Aristotle passage is from his discussion of whether friends are needed more in good or bad fortune; it is applied by analogy. The repeat screen flags narayana-murthy-infosys-founding-ten-thousand-rupees-1981 as 'same-founder', apparently because both founder fields name a founder plus unnamed co-founders; it is a different person, company and episode, and no field was changed.
